## Background
John's Gospel is traditionally attributed to John the apostle, "the disciple whom Jesus loved," and is usually dated to about AD 85 to 95. It was written so that readers "might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God" and have life through his name (John 20:31). This chapter is set early in Jesus' ministry, in Jerusalem and then the Judean countryside, while John the Baptist was still preaching and baptizing. Nicodemus is a Pharisee and "a ruler of the Jews," probably a member of the leading Jewish council. He is a respected teacher of Israel's Scriptures.

## What happens
Nicodemus comes to Jesus at night and honors him as a teacher sent from God, pointing to his miracles (vv. 1–2). Jesus answers that no one can see God's kingdom without being "born again" (v. 3). Nicodemus takes this literally and asks how an old man could re-enter his mother's womb (v. 4). Jesus explains that a person must be born "of water and of the Spirit" (v. 5). Flesh produces flesh, but the Spirit gives a new kind of life. That life is as real and as mysterious as the wind, which you hear but cannot trace (vv. 6–8).

Nicodemus is still puzzled (v. 9). Jesus gently rebukes Israel's teacher for not understanding (v. 10) and says he speaks as one who has come down from heaven (vv. 11–13). Then he points ahead. Just as Moses lifted up a serpent in the wilderness, the Son of Man must be "lifted up" so that believers may have eternal life (vv. 14–15).

Verses 16–21 announce that God so loved the world that he gave his only Son. He sent him to save the world, not to condemn it. Judgment comes when people prefer darkness to light because they fear their deeds will be exposed. Those who do the truth come to the light. Translations differ on whether these verses are still Jesus speaking or the Gospel writer reflecting.

The scene then shifts to Judea, where Jesus' disciples are baptizing while John baptizes at Aenon (vv. 22–24). John's followers, unsettled after a dispute about purification, complain that crowds are now going to Jesus (vv. 25–26). John replies that everything is a gift from heaven. He is not the Christ, only the friend of the bridegroom, who rejoices at the groom's voice. "He must increase, but I must decrease" (vv. 27–30). The chapter closes by declaring that the one from above speaks God's words, has the Spirit without measure and holds all things from the Father. Whoever believes in the Son has everlasting life (vv. 31–36).

## Key words and ideas
- Born again: the Greek word can mean "again" or "from above." Both senses fit: a new start that comes from God. Nicodemus hears only the first.
- Water and the Spirit: Catholic, Orthodox, and many Lutheran and Anglican readers understand "water" as pointing to baptism. Many other Protestants read it as spiritual cleansing, or as natural birth alongside spiritual birth.
- Lifted up: in John this phrase points to Jesus being raised on the cross, which is also the path to his glory.
- Light and darkness: belief is not only an idea. It shows in whether people come toward God's truth or hide from it.

## Connections
Numbers 21:7–9 tells how Israelites bitten by serpents looked at the bronze serpent Moses raised and lived. Jesus uses this as a picture of himself in verse 14. Ezekiel 36:25–27 promises clean water and a new spirit for God's people, which may be what Nicodemus should have recognized. 1 Peter 1:23–25 speaks of being born again through God's lasting word. Genesis 22:12 recalls Abraham not withholding his only son, which echoes "he gave his only begotten Son." Romans 5:8 says God shows his love in that Christ died for us while we were still sinners. Luke 19:10 matches verse 17: the Son came to seek and save the lost.

## For reflection
- What questions might you bring to Jesus "by night," privately and honestly?
- What does it mean to you that God sent his Son to save rather than to condemn?
- Where might God be asking you to "decrease" so that Christ can increase?
